arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Givens argued six prestatehood acts defeated Idaho's title to submerged lands.
Mr. Strack argued submerged lands are an essential attribute of state sovereignty.
Mr. Strack noted the Corps of Engineers does not typically regulate state encroachments.
Justice O'Connor asked if the Corps could preempt state regulation of state interests.

paragraphs: Idaho argues six prestatehood acts defeated its title to submerged lands. The United States counters that submerged lands are essential to state sovereignty. The Court must decide which legal principle controls the dispute.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Idaho wants the Court to find its title to submerged lands was defeated before statehood.
The United States wants the Court to affirm that submerged lands are essential to state sovereignty.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Chief Justice Rehnquist asked Mr. Givens to clarify his statement about prestatehood acts.
Justice O'Connor asked Mr. Strack about federal preemption when state interests are involved.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The outcome determines who controls submerged lands in Idaho. This affects state management of waterways and federal regulatory authority. The decision clarifies the balance between state sovereignty and federal power over submerged lands.
